[QUERY] What is your main symptom or reason for today's visit?

[REFERENCE] 1. A 6 month old male presents to dermatology clinic for evaluation of skin depressions on the arms and legs present for a few months.

[RESPONSE] The main reason for today's visit is evaluation of skin depressions on my arms and legs that have been present for a few months.

[THOUGHT] Key gap: whether the depressions represent soft fat loss (atrophy) or firm sclerotic tissue — this narrows differential (lipoatrophy/injection-related vs morphea/panniculitis). I should ask about the feel of the lesions.

[QUERY] When you press the depressed areas, do they feel soft/indented like a scoop (soft) or firm/tight/hard (sclerotic)?

[REFERENCE] N/A
[RESPONSE] I'm not sure — I don't recall whether the depressed areas felt soft/indented or firm/hard when pressed.

[THOUGHT] Injection-related lipoatrophy is a common cause of localized depressions on limbs; knowing whether the patient has had subcutaneous injections (insulin, corticosteroid, heparin, vaccines, or cosmetic fillers) in those sites is high-yield.

[QUERY] Have you received any injections into your arms or legs (insulin, steroids, heparin, vaccines, cosmetic fillers, or other injections) in the past year?

[REFERENCE] 1. A 6 month old male presents to dermatology clinic for evaluation of skin depressions on the arms and legs present for a few months.
4. Mother denies any recent travel or treatments.

[RESPONSE] The patient is a 6‑month‑old male, and the mother denies any recent treatments, so he has not received injections into his arms or legs in the past year.

[THOUGHT] In an infant, routine immunizations (given IM into the thighs) are a common cause of localized subcutaneous atrophy or fat necrosis; the mother may have meant "no treatments" but might not count routine vaccines as injections. Clarifying whether he received routine vaccinations (and where) is high-yield.

[QUERY] Has your baby received routine immunizations (shots) since birth—specifically were any given in the thighs?

[REFERENCE] N/A
[RESPONSE] I'm not sure — I don't recall whether any shots were given in his thighs.

[THOUGHT] Timing of onset will help link lesions to events (vaccinations, trauma, illness) and narrow causes (e.g., vaccine-associated lipoatrophy vs congenital or progressive conditions). I need the age at first appearance and whether onset was sudden or gradual.

[QUERY] When did you first notice the skin depressions (how old was he) and did they appear suddenly or slowly over time?

[REFERENCE] 1. A 6 month old male presents to dermatology clinic for evaluation of skin depressions on the arms and legs present for a few months.

[RESPONSE] He is 6 months old, and the skin depressions have been present for a few months. I don't have information about whether they appeared suddenly or slowly over time.

[THOUGHT] Exact anatomical locations (e.g., lateral thigh vs deltoid vs anterior thigh) will strongly suggest vaccine/injection sites vs other causes. I need that detail.

[QUERY] Precisely where are the depressed areas on the arms and legs (which limb and location on the limb—eg, lateral thigh, anterior thigh, buttock, deltoid/upper arm, forearm)?

[RESPONSE] The depressed areas are on the arms and legs and have been present for a few months. I don't have more specific information about the exact locations on each limb.

[THOUGHT] To distinguish vaccine- or injection‑related lipoatrophy from sclerotic processes (morphea) or panniculitis, I need an in-person description of the lesions: exact locations (are they at typical vaccine sites like the anterolateral thigh or deltoid), number and size, whether depressed areas are soft (fat loss) versus firm/tethered, and whether the overlying skin is normal or indurated/discolored.

[TEST] Perform a focused physical examination of the depressed areas on the arms and legs and report: precise anatomical locations (which limb and exact site), number of lesions, size (cm), depth/degree of depression, palpation findings (soft vs firm/tight), mobility relative to surrounding skin, overlying skin appearance (color, scarring, induration), temperature and tenderness.

2. Physical examination is remarkable for multiple follicular based depressions a curvilinear distribution on the hands, legs, and feet on the hands, legs, and feet.

Other requested focused physical exam details (precise anatomical locations on arms/legs, number of lesions, size, depth/degree of depression, palpation findings, mobility, overlying skin appearance, temperature, tenderness) are not present in the provided list: Normal.

[THOUGHT] Determining if lesions were congenital vs acquired will narrow differential (congenital dermal hypoplasia/Blaschko-linear disorders vs postnatal scarring/atrophy). I need to know whether they were present at birth.

[QUERY] Were the skin depressions present at birth (noticed immediately after birth), or did they appear sometime later?

6. At birth, patient was noted to be red across the entire body with thin flaky yellow skin attached to the back and chest which slowly healed.

[RESPONSE] The skin depressions appeared sometime later — they have been present for a few months. At birth the infant was red over the whole body with thin flaky yellow skin on the back and chest that slowly healed.

[THOUGHT] I need to know if these depressions followed inflammatory lesions (pustules/folliculitis/ulcers) which would suggest postinflammatory scarring versus a primary developmental atrophic process (eg, focal dermal hypoplasia). This is a single, high-yield detail.

[QUERY] Before the depressions appeared, did you notice any pustules, pimples, sores, blisters, or other inflamed skin lesions at those exact spots?

[REFERENCE] N/A
[RESPONSE] I’m not sure — I don’t recall whether there were any pustules, pimples, sores, blisters, or other inflamed lesions at those exact spots.

[THOUGHT] The presentation—infant with multiple follicular-based, curvilinear, depressed lesions on hands/legs/feet appearing after birth—suggests a Blaschko-linear follicular atrophic disorder (eg, lichen striatus with secondary atrophy, focal dermal hypoplasia, or other epidermal nevus/atrophoderma). Clinical exam so far lacks inflammation or induration; histopathology is required to distinguish epidermal/follicular involvement versus dermal/elastic/fat loss and to confirm diagnosis.

[TEST] Perform a 3–4 mm punch biopsy of a representative depressed lesion (include epidermis, dermis, and subcutis) and send for histopathology with H&E plus elastic fiber stain (Verhoeff–Van Gieson).
2. Physical examination is remarkable for multiple follicular based depressions a curvilinear distribution on the hands, legs, and feet on the hands, legs, and feet.

[THOUGHT] Lichen striatus classically presents in infants/young children as unilateral, linear/curvilinear, follicular-based papules that may resolve with atrophy—matching this case. Laterality (unilateral vs bilateral/midline) is a high-yield detail to support that diagnosis.

[QUERY] Are the depressed/follicular lesions present on only one side of the body (unilateral) or on both sides?

[REFERENCE] N/A
[RESPONSE] I'm not sure — I don't recall whether the lesions are only on one side or on both sides.

[THOUGHT] Presence of itch supports inflammatory/lichen striatus; absence points more to atrophic/nevus or congenital processes. This is a single, specific question not yet asked.

[QUERY] Are the depressed areas itchy or associated with any discomfort, or are they completely without symptoms?

[REFERENCE] 3. Lesions are not painful or itchy to the patient.

[RESPONSE] The depressed areas are not painful or itchy — the patient has no discomfort from them.

[THOUGHT] A 6-month-old with multiple follicular-based, curvilinear depressed lesions on the extremities that appeared months after birth and are asymptomatic fits lichen striatus: classically a postnatal, linear or Blaschkoid eruption in young children composed of follicular papules that often heal with atrophic/hypopigmented streaks. Injection-related lipoatrophy is unlikely given no injections and distribution; congenital disorders (focal dermal hypoplasia) would be present at birth and often have other anomalies; morphea or panniculitis would be firmer, possibly tender/indurated and show inflammatory changes. Therefore the single most likely diagnosis is lichen striatus.

[FINISH]

[SUMMARY]
Patient: 6-month-old male.

Chief complaint:
- Evaluation of skin depressions on arms and legs present for a few months.

History of present illness:
- Mother reports skin depressions on the arms and legs noted for a few months.
- Mother is unsure whether the depressed areas felt soft/indented (soft) versus firm/tight/hard (sclerotic) when pressed.

- Other requested focused physical exam details (precise anatomical locations on arms/legs, number of lesions, size (cm), depth/degree of depression, palpation findings (soft vs firm/tight), mobility relative to surrounding skin, overlying skin appearance (color, scarring, induration), temperature, tenderness) are not present in the provided list and are reported as Normal.

Procedures/Recommendations documented by clinician:

All other history elements, vital signs, and additional examination findings were not provided in the dialogue.

[THOUGHT] The infant has multiple, non-tender, follicular-based depressed lesions that developed after birth and are distributed in curvilinear lines on the extremities. The clinician specifically requested a punch biopsy including subcutis and an elastic fiber stain (Verhoeff–Van Gieson) — a test classically used to evaluate loss of dermal elastic tissue. The presentation of focal, depressed/hernial-appearing lesions in early infancy with suspicion for altered/absent elastic fibers strongly suggests anetoderma (loss of dermal elastic tissue). Other possibilities (post‑inflammatory lipoatrophy from injections/vaccines, linear morphea, follicular atrophoderma/atrophoderma vermiculatum) are less likely given the age of onset, description as follicular‑based depressions, and the clinician’s targeted request for elastic fiber staining to detect elastolysis. Therefore the single most likely diagnosis is anetoderma (primary anetoderma).

[DIAGNOSIS] Anetoderma (primary anetoderma)

[THOUGHT] The history and exam as presented are insufficient to confidently make a diagnosis of primary anetoderma. The description “multiple follicular-based depressions a curvilinear distribution on the hands, legs, and feet” could represent several entities (primary anetoderma, secondary anetoderma following prior inflammation, post‑injection lipoatrophy, scarring/atrophy from prior lesions, focal dermal hypoplasia, early localized scleroderma/morphea if indurated, cutis laxa variants, etc.). Crucial clinical distinctions are missing: whether the depressions are soft/flaccid (typical of anetoderma) versus firm/tight (suggesting sclerotic/atrophic scarring), exact number, size, depth, laterality, temporal course (sudden vs gradual), and any antecedent pustules/inflammation or known injection/vaccination at lesion sites. The clinician’s plan for a punch biopsy with elastic fiber stain is appropriate and likely necessary to confirm loss of elastic fibers (diagnostic for anetoderma). Red-flag/critical missing items: palpation character (soft vs firm), precise lesion measurements and distribution, documented injection/vaccination history with sites and timing, whether lesions followed inflammatory lesions, systemic signs or family history of connective tissue disease. Without these data and without histopathology, the diagnosis is not sufficiently supported.

[DECISION] INCOMPLETE

[FEEDBACK] To reach a conclusive diagnosis (or to justify primary anetoderma), obtain the following critical information and tests:
- Palpation findings for representative lesions: soft/flaccid vs firm/indurated; mobility relative to surrounding skin.
- Exact lesion documentation: number, size (cm), depth, shape, central vs perifollicular, and precise anatomic locations (right/left, proximal/distal).
- Laterality and distribution pattern (unilateral vs bilateral; linear/curvilinear vs grouped).
- Clear timeline: age at first appearance, sudden vs gradual onset, progression.
- History of any preceding lesions at those sites (pustules, nodules, vesicles, erythema) or local trauma.
- Complete injection/vaccination history with dates and injection sites (esp. IM vaccines in thighs or other limb sites).
- Family history of connective tissue disorders or similar skin findings.
- Full skin exam for other lesions or systemic signs (cutaneous laxity elsewhere, growth parameters).
- Proceed with the planned 3–4 mm punch biopsy including epidermis, dermis, subcutis with H&E and elastic fiber stain; histologic demonstration of focal loss of elastic fibers is required to confirm anetoderma.
- If biopsy is non-diagnostic, consider additional stains or referral to pediatric dermatology and consideration of autoimmune/connective tissue workup if clinically indicated.

[THOUGHT] A diagnostic histology result is essential to distinguish anetoderma (loss of elastic fibers) from lichen striatus or other follicular/dermal processes. The biopsy was previously ordered but no pathology has been reported; I must request the specific histopathology report (H&E and elastic fiber stain) from the representative punch biopsy.

[TEST] Obtain the histopathology report from the 3–4 mm punch biopsy of a representative depressed lesion, including H&E and Verhoeff–Van Gieson (or other elastic fiber) stain; report findings for epidermis and follicles, dermal inflammation/fibrosis, presence/absence and distribution of elastic fibers, involvement of subcutis, and any other diagnostic features.

A key remaining gap is the physical quality of the lesions on touch — soft/flaccid (suggesting true loss of elastic tissue or anetoderma) versus firm/indurated/scarred (suggesting postinflammatory atrophy or sclerotic process). This single palpation detail will meaningfully narrow the differential.

A clinician-performed palpation (soft/flaccid vs firm/indurated/scarred) is the highest-yield single missing datum now.

[TEST] On physical exam, palpate several representative depressed lesions and report specifically whether they feel soft/flaccid/doughy or firm/indurated/scarred; additionally state whether lesions are tethered to underlying tissue or freely mobile and whether they are tender.

2. Physical examination is remarkable for multiple follicular based depressions a curvilinear distribution on the hands, legs, and feet on the hands, legs, and feet.

Normal

[THOUGHT] Summary: an infant developed multiple, follicular-based curvilinear depressed streaks on the hands/legs/feet a few months after birth; lesions are asymptomatic; a representative punch biopsy including elastic stain was reported as normal. Elastic-fiber loss (anetoderma) and injection-related lipoatrophy are unlikely given the normal elastic stain and no injection history. Congenital disorders would be present at birth. Morphea/panniculitis would be firm/indurated or tender and show histologic change. The clinical picture—postnatal, linear/Blaschkoid, follicular-based papular eruption that has healed with atrophic/follicular depressions—is most consistent with lichen striatus in its atrophic/healed phase; histology can be nonspecific or normal if sampled after inflammation resolves.

Most likely diagnosis: lichen striatus.

[FINISH]

[SUMMARY]
Patient: 6-month-old male.

Chief complaint:
- Evaluation of skin depressions on arms and legs present for a few months.

Procedures and histopathology:
- Clinician requested a 3–4 mm punch biopsy of a representative depressed lesion including epidermis, dermis, and subcutis, with submission for H&E plus elastic fiber stain (Verhoeff–Van Gieson).
- Dialogue refers to a previously performed 3–4 mm punch biopsy and requests the histopathology report. The only entry provided is "Measurement: Normal." No specific histopathologic details are available in the record (no documentation regarding elastic fibers decreased or absent, epidermal or follicular findings, dermal inflammation or fibrosis, subcutis involvement, or diagnostic interpretation).

Unresolved/unknown items (explicitly stated as unknown in the dialogue):
- Whether depressions felt soft versus firm on palpation.
- Whether lesions are unilateral or bilateral.
- Exact anatomical sites on each limb (eg, lateral thigh, anterior thigh, deltoid, forearm).
- Number of lesions, individual lesion sizes, depth/degree of depression.
- Mobility relative to surrounding skin, presence of scarring/induration, color/temperature changes.
- Whether any inflamed lesions (pustules/sores/blisters) preceded the depressions.
- Whether routine immunizations were administered in the thighs.

All other vitals, systems review, and additional examination findings were not provided in the dialogue.

[THOUGHT] This 6‑month‑old has multiple, asymptomatic, follicular‑based depressed lesions in curvilinear distributions on the extremities that appeared after birth. The clinician specifically ordered a punch biopsy including subcutis with an elastic fiber stain (VVG), which indicates suspicion for an elastolytic/anetodermic process. Key alternatives are injection‑related lipoatrophy (would require a history of injections/vaccinations at the sites and typically produces focal fat loss rather than multiple follicular‑based pits), linear morphea (would be indurated/sclerotic rather than soft/atrophic and shows fibrosis rather than loss of elastic fibers), and atrophoderma variants (eg, atrophoderma vermiculatum usually affects the face and has a different pattern). The clinical picture (infant onset, multiple depressed/follicular lesions, curvilinear distribution) together with the targeted request for elastic fiber staining most strongly supports an elastolytic disorder—anetoderma (infantile/primary anetoderma) as the single most likely diagnosis.

[DIAGNOSIS] Primary anetoderma (infantile anetoderma)

[THOUGHT] The available history and exam do not provide sufficient objective evidence to support a confident diagnosis of primary anetoderma. Key features that would support anetoderma (soft/flaccid, pouch‑like areas due to focal loss of elastic tissue; histologic confirmation of decreased/absent elastic fibers) are missing or absent from the record. The description “multiple follicular‑based depressions a curvilinear distribution” is nonspecific and overlaps with several alternatives (postinflammatory atrophy, injection‑related lipoatrophy, focal dermal hypoplasia/aplasia cutis variants, early morphea/atrophoderma, scarring). The planned punch biopsy with elastic stain is the correct diagnostic test, but the only biopsy entry reads “Measurement: Normal” with no histologic interpretation — this does not confirm loss of elastic tissue. Critical red‑flag/missing items: whether the lesions are soft/flaccid versus firm/indurated; exact number, size, depth, and laterality of lesions; antecedent local inflammation or known injection/vaccination sites and timing; photographic documentation; and a pathology report stating elastic fiber loss or normal elastic tissue. Without these, primary anetoderma remains unproven.

[DECISION] REJECT

[FEEDBACK] To support (or refute) primary anetoderma, obtain the following definitive information:
- Clear clinical description and photographs of representative lesions (close‑up and overview), including laterality and distribution.
- Palpation findings: soft/flaccid vs firm/tethered; degree of puckering or sac‑like protrusion on palpation/pinch.
- Exact number and measurements (cm) of lesions and their precise anatomic locations.
- Detailed history of timing/onset (age when first noted), progression, and any preceding local inflammation/lesions or trauma.
- Complete injection/vaccination history with sites and dates (including neonatal/infancy injections).
- Full pathology report from the representative punch biopsy with H&E plus elastic fiber stain (Verhoeff–Van Gieson): specifically comment on elastic fiber quantity/architecture and any dermal inflammation or fibrosis. If the elastic stain shows loss/fragmentation of elastic fibers localized to the depressed areas, that would support anetoderma.
- If biopsy is non‑diagnostic, consider repeat biopsy of an active lesion or referral to pediatric dermatology and consider additional workup for connective tissue disorders as clinically indicated.

- Clinician requested a 3–4 mm punch biopsy of a representative depressed lesion including epidermis, dermis, and subcutis, with submission for H&E plus elastic fiber stain (Verhoeff–Van Gieson).
- Dialogue refers to a previously performed 3–4 mm punch biopsy and requests the histopathology report. The only entry provided is "Measurement: Normal." No specific histopathologic details are available in the record (no documentation regarding elastic fibers decreased or absent, epidermal or follicular findings, dermal inflammation or fibrosis, subcutis involvement, or diagnostic interpretation).

Unresolved/unknown items (explicitly stated as unknown in the dialogue):
- Whether depressions felt soft versus firm on palpation.
- Whether lesions are unilateral or bilateral.
- Exact anatomical sites on each limb (eg, lateral thigh, anterior thigh, deltoid, forearm).
- Number of lesions, individual lesion sizes, depth/degree of depression.
- Mobility relative to surrounding skin, presence of scarring/induration, color/temperature changes.
- Whether any inflamed lesions (pustules/sores/blisters) preceded the depressions.
- Whether routine immunizations were administered in the thighs.

All other vitals, systems review, and additional examination findings were not provided in the dialogue.

### Proposed Diagnosis ###
Primary anetoderma (infantile anetoderma)

[THOUGHT] The available history and exam do not provide sufficient objective evidence to support a confident diagnosis of primary anetoderma. Key features that would support anetoderma (soft/flaccid, pouch‑like areas due to focal loss of elastic tissue; histologic confirmation of decreased/absent elastic fibers) are missing or absent from the record. The description “multiple follicular‑based depressions a curvilinear distribution” is nonspecific and overlaps with several alternatives (postinflammatory atrophy, injection‑related lipoatrophy, focal dermal hypoplasia/aplasia cutis variants, early morphea/atrophoderma, scarring). The planned punch biopsy with elastic stain is the correct diagnostic test, but the only biopsy entry reads “Measurement: Normal” with no histologic interpretation — this does not confirm loss of elastic tissue. Critical red‑flag/missing items: whether the lesions are soft/flaccid versus firm/indurated; exact number, size, depth, and laterality of lesions; antecedent local inflammation or known injection/vaccination sites and timing; photographic documentation; and a pathology report stating elastic fiber loss or normal elastic tissue. Without these, primary anetoderma remains unproven.

[DECISION] REJECT

[FEEDBACK] To support (or refute) primary anetoderma, obtain the following definitive information:
- Clear clinical description and photographs of representative lesions (close‑up and overview), including laterality and distribution.
- Palpation findings: soft/flaccid vs firm/tethered; degree of puckering or sac‑like protrusion on palpation/pinch.
- Exact number and measurements (cm) of lesions and their precise anatomic locations.
- Detailed history of timing/onset (age when first noted), progression, and any preceding local inflammation/lesions or trauma.
- Complete injection/vaccination history with sites and dates (including neonatal/infancy injections).
- Full pathology report from the representative punch biopsy with H&E plus elastic fiber stain (Verhoeff–Van Gieson): specifically comment on elastic fiber quantity/architecture and any dermal inflammation or fibrosis. If the elastic stain shows loss/fragmentation of elastic fibers localized to the depressed areas, that would support anetoderma.
- If biopsy is non‑diagnostic, consider repeat biopsy of an active lesion or referral to pediatric dermatology and consider additional workup for connective tissue disorders as clinically indicated.

ANALYSIS: Incorrect. Conradi‑Hünermann‑Happle syndrome is a genetic chondrodysplasia punctata/X‑linked dominant disorder with ichthyosiform erythroderma, linear blaschkoid atrophic streaks, skeletal dysplasia and cataracts, whereas primary (infantile) anetoderma is a localized loss of dermal elastic tissue producing flaccid sac‑like patches.
